relations.subject: n1ql:fn-search
relations.reused_or_minted_predicate: reused - promoted predicate; this is a relaxation of a prior requirement rather than a new feature, so behavesDifferentlyUnder fits better than availableSince
relations.evidence: From Couchbase Server 7.6 and later, when you use the SEARCH function, you do not need to use the [keyword analyzer](../../search/default-analyzers-reference.md#keyword) in your Search index to run a non-analytic query. You also do not need to match the analyzer in a query to the analyzer in the Search index for an analytic query.

relations.subject: n1ql:fn-meta

SQL++ cannot return XATTRs data without a specific field name.

relations.subject: n1ql:fn-search-meta
relations.reused_or_minted_predicate: reused - promoted predicate; the complementary condition to the relation above ('If you do have a Search index available')

You must also include the [fields property](../../search/search-request-params.md#fields) with the name of the XATTRs field in your Search request.

relations.subject: n1ql:fn-search
relations.reused_or_minted_predicate: reused - the documented trade-off is that when no suitable Search index exists the query still succeeds, but at a performance cost paid in the Search Service
relations.evidence: If no suitable Search index can be selected, or no Search index exists, the Query engine falls back on a Primary index or qualified GSI index to produce document keys, and then fetches the documents. The Search Service then creates a temporary index in memory to perform the search. This process may be slower than using a suitable Search index.

relations.subject: n1ql:fn-search
relations.reused_or_minted_predicate: reused - a genuine cross-component behaviour divergence: the *same* Full Text Search request object is honoured differently depending on whether it is issued through SQL++ or directly to the Search Service. Object is a service rather than a version, which stretches the predicate's usual usage - flagged for reconciliation
relations.evidence: When specifying a complete Full Text Search request with the SQL++ SEARCH() function, if the value of the size parameter is greater than the [maximum number of Full Text Search results](../../fts/fts-search-response.md), the query ignores the size parameter and returns all matching results. This is different to the behavior of a complete Full Text Search request in the Search Service, where the query returns an error if the value of the size parameter is greater than the maximum number of Full Text Search results.

notable_absence.finding: No edition gate anywhere on this page, even though the page documents Vector Search (a knn object inside the SEARCH() query argument) and vector search is Enterprise-gated on other pages in this wave (see server/current/n1ql/n1ql-language-reference/createindex.json, which records requiresEdition edition:enterprise for vector index features). If SEARCH()-with-knn is in fact Enterprise-only, this page does not say so; if it is not, that is a notable asymmetry with CREATE INDEX. Either way it is a gap the reader cannot resolve from this page.

cross_component_finding: This is the clearest dependsOnService page in the batch: it is a Query Service reference page whose entire subject matter is delegation to the Search Service ('The Query engine then passes the search specification over to the Search engine to perform the search'), and it documents three distinct cross-component behaviours worth modelling as first-class facts rather than prose: (1) the fallback path when no Search index is available, where the Query Service produces keys from a Primary or GSI index and the Search Service builds a temporary in-memory index; (2) the index-selection interaction, where a SEARCH() predicate disables GSI covering scans on that keyspace entirely ('If the SEARCH() function is present for a keyspace, no GSI covering scan is possible on that keyspace'); and (3) the size-parameter divergence between the SQL++ and native-Search request paths, captured as a relation above. The page also reaches into the Search module for index definitions, analyzers, and index UUIDs, and into the Index Service for the GSI/primary fallback - three services named on one function-reference page.
cross_product_finding: The divergence here runs the *opposite* way to what the brief anticipated. The Capella twin (cloud/n1ql/n1ql-language-reference/searchfun.md) carries MORE version-gating text than the Server 8.0 page, not less: Capella titles two of its worked examples '(Version 7.6.2) Search with XATTRs data and no suitable Search index' and '(Version 7.6.2) Search with XATTRs data and a specific Search index', and hedges the surrounding prose with 'If your cluster is running Couchbase Server version 7.6.2 and there is no suitable Search index...' and 'If your cluster is running Couchbase Server version 7.6.2 or later and you want to return XATTRs data...'. The Server 8.0 page has stripped all four of those version qualifiers, keeping only the single 'When to Use Search Functions' sentence. This is presumably deliberate - on an 8.0 page a 7.6.2 gate is always satisfied - but the consequence is that the *versionless* product page is the better source of availableSince evidence than the versioned one, which is exactly backwards for anyone harvesting version facts from server/current. Second, and smaller: the authorization sentence is word-for-word identical in both products ('The role **Data Admin** must be assigned...'), so this page is a rare case where the Server RBAC model and the Capella access model are stated in the *same* terms; the Capella extraction record filed those roles under requiresPrivilege and I have filed them under requiresRole. Reconciliation must pick one, and should not read the difference as a product difference - it is an extractor difference.
version_finding: Two harvestable gates on this page: n1ql:xattrs-in-query availableSince version:server-7-6-2, and a relaxation of the Search-index analyzer requirement at version:server-7-6 (captured as behavesDifferentlyUnder, since nothing new became available - a prior requirement was dropped). The 7.6 case is a useful test of the wave's vocabulary: 'you do not need to use the keyword analyzer' is a *removed constraint*, which is neither availableSince nor deprecatedIn. If reconciliation wants to distinguish 'feature added' from 'requirement lifted', behavesDifferentlyUnder is currently the only available home for the latter and is already carrying two quite different jobs on this one page (a version-keyed behaviour change and a service-keyed behaviour difference). A dedicated predicate such as requirementLiftedIn may be worth minting. Separately: 'docid_regexp isn't supported yet' is a forward-looking soft claim with no version attached - it is not a deprecation and not an availability gate, and there is currently no vocabulary for 'not yet supported'.
